Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Insurance Holdings Q3 2023 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Jenkins, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Insurance Holdings' Q3 2023 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Rivera, Chief Financial Officer; Elena Vasquez, Chief Underwriting Officer; and David Kwon, Chief Investment Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we are making today may be considered forward-looking. These statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from those projected. We encourage you to review our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks and uncertainties.

I will now turn the call over to Johnathan Hale.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on Apex Insurance Holdings' performance for Q3 2023. We delivered strong results, driven by robust premium growth, disciplined expense management, favorable actuarial updates, manageable catastrophe impacts, and prudent capital returns through dividends and share repurchases. Our focus on digital transformation and risk selection continues to yield positive outcomes across our property and casualty, life, and specialty lines.

Michael, our CFO, will now provide a more detailed review of our financial performance.

Michael Rivera: Thank you, Johnathan. Good morning, everyone. As Johnathan mentioned, we had a solid quarter. Our net income was $750 million, or $2.37 per share. Key drivers of our financial performance included 14% constant currency premium growth, favorable reserve releases from actuarial assumption changes, and continued expense ratio compression. Our combined ratio was 92.8%, reflecting effective underwriting and claims management. Investment income for the quarter was $420 million, benefiting from higher yields on our fixed income portfolio. We continue to maintain a strong capital position, with risk-based capital ratio at 620%.

Turning now to our expense discipline, where we continue to demonstrate the operational leverage inherent in our business model. Our expense ratio for the quarter came in at 28.7%, a 110 basis point improvement year-over-year from 29.8% in Q3 last year, and sequentially down 20 basis points from Q2's 28.9%. This marks the fifth consecutive quarter of expense ratio compression, bringing our trailing 12-month ratio to a best-in-class 28.4%—well below the industry average of around 31% as reported by AM Best for composite P&C carriers.

For context, our expense ratio is calculated as the sum of our policy acquisition costs—primarily commissions and other underwriting expenses—and general and administrative expenses, divided by net earned premiums. Excluding the onetime $15 million restructuring charge we took in Q1 for optimizing our legacy IT systems, our core expense ratio would have been an even stronger 28.2%. This performance underscores our relentless focus on cost efficiency amid a challenging macro environment, including persistent inflation in repair costs—up 8% year-over-year per the CPI for motor vehicles—and elevated catastrophe activity, which pressured loss ratios across the industry.

Let me break this down by key drivers, starting with commission expenses, which represent about 43% of our total expense ratio, or 12.3% of earned premiums this quarter—down from 13.1% a year ago. This compression was driven by a favorable shift in our distribution mix. Direct-to-consumer channels, powered by our mobile app and embedded insurance partnerships with fintechs like Affirm and Klarna, now account for 32% of new business premiums, up from 25% last year. These digital sales bypass traditional agent commissions, which averaged 15-18% for personal lines like auto and home, versus under 2% for direct. In our U.S. P&C segment, for instance, we grew direct auto policies by 22% quarter-over-quarter, leveraging usage-based insurance telematics similar to Progressive's Snapshot program, which not only lowers acquisition costs but also improves risk selection.

Bancassurance also played a role, contributing 18% of life and health premiums in EMEA, where commissions run at 10-12% versus 20%+ for independent brokers. However, we did see some offset from higher variable commissions in our commercial lines, where broker commissions ticked up to 14.5% due to competitive pricing in middle-market property amid softening rates—think along the lines of what we've seen in the U.S. with AIG and Chubb chasing market share post-hardened rates.

Shifting to operating costs, which comprise the balance of our expense ratio at 16.4% of premiums—flat sequentially but down 90 basis points YoY—the story is one of disciplined G&A management and technology-enabled efficiencies. Headcount grew only 1.2% year-to-date to 12,500 globally, despite 14% premium growth, thanks to our zero-based budgeting approach and offshoring 15% of back-office functions to our Manila shared services center. Salaries and benefits rose 5% nominally but declined 2% as a percentage of premiums due to operating leverage.

A major tailwind here has been our multi-year digital transformation, Project Horizon, now in Phase 3. We've migrated 85% of our claims processing to a cloud-based platform using AWS and Guidewire's PolicyCenter, reducing manual handling by 40%. AI-driven fraud detection, powered by tools like those from Shift Technology—our partner since 2022—flagged $45 million in suspicious claims this quarter, cutting loss adjustment expenses embedded in our expense ratio by 15%. In auto claims, straight-through processing rates hit 72%, up from 55% two years ago, directly shaving 25 basis points off the ratio.

Regionally, performance varied as expected. In North America, which is 52% of premiums, our expense ratio improved to 27.9% from 29.5%, driven by scale in California homeowners post-wildfire reforms and Florida's Citizens depopulation efforts. Direct channel penetration here is highest at 38%, but we faced headwinds from rising litigation costs in no-fault states like New York, where legal defense fees within LAE increased 12%. EMEA saw a slight uptick to 29.2% from 28.8%, pressured by GDPR compliance investments—€20 million YTD—and higher energy transition commissions for parametric products covering wind farm downtime, akin to Allstate's renewable offerings. Conversely, Asia-Pacific delivered our strongest result at 28.1%, down 150 basis points, fueled by bancassurance growth in Indonesia and Vietnam, where low commissions (8-10%) and rapid premium scaling from motor two-wheelers offset typhoon-related claims spikes.

Commercial lines warrant a callout: expense ratio at 26.8%, benefiting from our facultative reinsurance partnerships with Swiss Re, which deferred $30 million in acquisition costs via DAC amortization extensions under IFRS 17. This contrasts with personal lines at 29.5%, where marketing spend rose modestly to support UBI adoption amid softening competition from Lemonade and Hippo.

Strategically, we're not resting on these gains. We've set a 2025 target of 27.5% through three levers: further direct mix shift to 40% via API integrations with ride-sharing platforms like Uber for on-demand coverage; GenAI pilots in underwriting, expected to automate 60% of small commercial quotes by year-end, mirroring Zurich's successes; and synergies from our pending Travelers bolt-on acquisition, projecting $50 million in annual G&A savings via platform consolidation. Reinsurance terms remain favorable, with our quota-share on U.S. catastrophe excess at 95% retention post-1-in-250-year events, limiting expense volatility.

Before moving on, I'd like to touch on our catastrophe loss experience, which remains a critical lens for understanding our P&C underwriting performance amid a volatile climate risk landscape. Total catastrophe losses for the quarter came in at $1.45 billion pre-tax, representing 4.2% of our gross written premium, or GWP, of $34.6 billion. This marks a 28% decline from the $2.02 billion, or 6.1% of GWP, we reported in Q3 2022, driven by a relatively benign North Atlantic hurricane season and our proactive portfolio actions.

Our cat losses are defined per industry convention as events exceeding $10 million per occurrence, net of reinsurance recoveries, and include both nat-cat perils like hurricanes, wildfires, and floods, as well as non-nat events like civil unrest where applicable. For Q3, the lion's share—62%, or $900 million—stemmed from U.S. personal and commercial property lines, primarily Hurricane Lee and residual claims from earlier wildfires in California akin to the 2022 McKinney Fire patterns. This equated to 3.8 points of loss ratio impact in our U.S. book, where GWP grew 5% YoY to $18.2 billion on strong commercial multi-peril and homeowners demand.

Regionally, Europe contributed $320 million, or 22% of the total, at 1.9% of regional GWP—elevated due to Storm Ciarán's wind and flood damages across the UK and Benelux, mirroring the €2 billion industry-wide hit estimated by EIOPA. Our motor and SME packages here absorbed much of it, but our 15% rate adequacy gains over the past 18 months kept the underlying loss ratio at 62%. In Asia-Pacific, typhoons in Japan and the Philippines drove $150 million, or 1.1% of APAC GWP, a 40% YoY drop thanks to our exit from high-exposure single-family home portfolios in Tokyo metro and a ramp-up in parametric triggers with partners like Descartes Underwriting.

Latin America and other regions rounded out at $80 million, negligible at 0.4% of GWP, underscoring the benefits of our geographic diversification strategy post-2021 Uruguay floods.

Year-to-date through Q3, cumulative cat losses stand at $4.1 billion, or 4.0% of YTD GWP of $102.8 billion—well below our five-year average of 5.3% and the Swiss Re sigma benchmark of 4.8% for global P&C markets. This has helped compress our accident year loss ratio ex-cat to 61.5%, supporting a Q3 combined ratio of 95.4%, our best in three years.

Frequency remains elevated—we've seen 17 named cat events YTD versus 14 last year—attributable to La Niña influences and secondary perils like severe convective storms, which punched 25% above the 10-year norm per Verisk Analytics. Climate attribution modeling from Gallagher Re shows a 15-20% increase in insured losses from warming trends, particularly in our $12 billion U.S. homeowners exposure.

On the mitigation front, we've leaned into technical initiatives that are paying off. First, our refreshed cat modeling platform, co-developed with Risk Management Solutions v18 models, incorporates probabilistic hurricane tracks and wildfire spread algorithms refined post-Irma/Maria. This led to a 12% reduction in probable maximum loss estimates for our Florida book, enabling us to retain $2.5 billion more risk on-balance sheet at optimized terms. Second, we upsized our global reinsurance program effective 1/1/23: our property cat tower now features a $1.75 billion XS layer at 1:250 return period, ceding 45% of gross cat risk versus 38% prior year, with favorable terms from Swiss Re and RenaissanceRe amid softening retrocession markets. We've also piloted AI-driven early warning systems with IBM Watson for SCS perils, slashing claims cycle times by 30% in Midwest pilots.

Strategically, these dynamics reinforce our fortress balance sheet approach. We've achieved 8.2% net pricing across renewing cat-exposed lines, outpacing 6.5% GWP growth, while reshaping exposures: U.S. Southeast homeowners down 7% via non-renewals in Miami-Dade; APAC industrial fire up 12% with IoT telematics mandates. Looking forward, we expect FY cat losses at 3.8-4.2% of GWP, assuming no top-10 industry event per AIR Worldwide's $105 billion global forecast. This positions us to harvest mid-teens ROEs, with excess capital deployment into bolt-on M&A like our recent $450 million acquisition of a cyber-cat specialist to hedge emerging risks.

Another key driver behind our reserve releases this quarter involves changes in actuarial assumptions and their impacts. As you know, actuarial assumptions are the backbone of our liability valuation under both US GAAP LDTI and our growing IFRS 17 portfolio in Europe and Asia. These include discount rates, mortality and morbidity improvements, policy lapse and persistency rates, expense margins, and emerging risks like climate-adjusted loss trends in our P&C lines.

Net favorable impacts from assumption updates totaled $285 million pre-tax this quarter, contributing approximately 12% to our bottom line beat of $2.37 per share. This brings our year-to-date favorable reserve releases to $620 million, up 25% from the prior year, driven by a combination of experience data maturation, macroeconomic tailwinds, and refined modeling techniques.

First, discount rates were the biggest swing factor this period. With the 10-year Treasury yield climbing 75 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 4.35%, we updated our risk-free rate curves across all lines. For our $45 billion life and annuity block—heavily weighted toward fixed indexed annuities similar to those offered by Athene or Corebridge—this resulted in a $210 million favorable unlock. Under LDTI's CSM framework, higher discounts reduce the present value of future benefit liabilities by about 2.8%, allowing us to accelerate CSM recognition into earnings. In our P&C segment, which represents 35% of reserves at $18 billion, the impact was more muted at $45 million due to shorter-tail commercial auto and workers' comp lines, but still supportive of our 92% combined ratio.

Regionally, this played out differently. In the US, where 70% of our annuity book resides, the Fed's hawkish pause amplified the benefit. Europe, under IFRS 17's more prescriptive discounting using EIOPA curves, saw a $60 million tailwind on our €12 billion UK and German life portfolio, offsetting some longevity strain. Asia-Pacific, our fastest-growing region at 15% YoY premium growth, experienced a neutral-to-favorable $25 million shift, as MAS rates aligned with our 3.2% blended discount assumption.

Second, mortality and morbidity assumptions: Post-COVID normalization continues to exceed expectations. Our updated Society of Actuaries Pri-2012 mortality table with scale improvements showed actual-to-expected ratios at 92% for group life—down from 105% in Q4 2022 peaks. This drove a $95 million reserve release on our $30 billion term life and critical illness block, akin to peers like Prudential or Lincoln National. Morbidity for long-term care improved marginally, with claim incidence 4% below prior assumptions, yielding $35 million favorable—a bright spot amid industry-wide LTC pressures.

However, we trended morbidity assumptions upward by 2.5% for disability income products, reflecting persistent inflation in medical costs (up 6.8% YoY per CMS data), adding a $20 million headwind. Climate risks factored in here too: for P&C catastrophe models, we widened loss cost trends by 1.2 percentage points in Florida and California exposures, incorporating RMS v18.0 scenarios, which increased hurricane deductibles reserves by $15 million but stayed within our $1.2 billion cat agg buffer.

Third, behavioral assumptions: lapses, persistency, and expenses. Lapse rates beat our models by 150 bps across universal life and whole life, at 4.8% realized vs. 6.3% assumed—thanks to sticky in-force books amid elevated living benefit riders, similar to Brighthouse Financial's strategies. This unlocked $45 million. Expense margins tightened 0.8% due to our $150 million tech spend on robotic process automation and cloud migration to Snowflake for actuarial data lakes, reducing admin costs to 18.5% of premiums.

Technical initiatives underpinning these changes: We're not just reacting; we're leading with innovation. Our Actuarial Modernization Program, Phase II, rolled out stochastic GLMs powered by Google Cloud AI, enabling 10,000-scenario runs in hours vs. weeks. This improved assumption credibility scores from 85% to 96% under SOA guidelines. We've also integrated alternative data sources like Verisk's climate analytics and Milliman's longevity projectors, reducing tail uncertainty by 15%. For IFRS 17 compliance in our €5 billion Asian universal life portfolio, we implemented BBA testing that shaved 3% off RA loadings.

Regional commentary: US (75% of reserves) saw dominant tailwinds from rates and mortality; P&C loss trends stable at 3.1% despite wildfire inflation. Europe (15%) had longevity creep—we've assumed 1.2 years further improvement per CMI 2023 models—pressuring UK annuities by $30 million unfavorably, but offset by €STR rate rises. Asia-Pac (10%) benefited from high persistency (95%+ on savings products) amid China's rate liberalization; we're stress-testing for 20% equity volatility per PBOC scenarios.

These updates affirm our disciplined pricing—our new business margins held at 22% pretax, outpacing industry averages per LIMRA data. We're derisking via reinsurance: $2.5 billion FIA quota share with Swiss Re at 105% recapture, and longevity swaps mirroring Legal & General's deals. Looking ahead, we expect Q4 neutral-to-$100 million favorable impacts, assuming 50 bps further rate upside, but monitor inflation (targeting CPI-linked escalators) and election-year regulatory shifts like NAIC's PBR enhancements.

As we wrap up our discussion on the quarter's results, I'd like to turn to one of our core commitments to shareholders: our dividend policy. We declared a sustainable payout of $0.68 per share for Q4, payable on December 15th to shareholders of record as of November 30th. This marks a 4.6% increase quarter-over-quarter from the $0.65 paid in Q3 and brings our trailing twelve-month dividend to $2.72 per share, up 5% year-over-year from $2.59 in 2022.

Our payout ratio stands at a healthy 42% of adjusted operating EPS for the TTM period, well within our target range of 35-50%. This leaves ample headroom for reinvestment and resilience against volatility—critical in our industry where catastrophe losses and investment spreads can swing quarter-to-quarter.

Looking at trends, we've delivered 12 consecutive years of dividend growth, with a 10-year CAGR of 4.2%—outpacing inflation and aligning with peers like Travelers and Chubb. This is anchored in our dividend capacity framework, which we stress-test annually under ORSA scenarios, including a 1-in-200-year cat event like Hurricane Ian's $65 billion industry-wide hit in 2022.

Regionally, this payout reflects divergent dynamics. In North America, which accounts for 65% of our $28 billion in GPW, robust commercial multi-peril and workers' comp renewals—up 7% in average premium per risk—have bolstered our statutory surplus by 8% YoY to $12.4 billion. This supports our ability to maintain and grow the dividend despite California wildfire season pressures, where we proactively non-renewed 15% of our highest-risk homeowners' policies in high-hazard zones. In EMEA, headwinds from inflationary repair costs and softer investment yields—our fixed income portfolio yielded 3.8% in Q3, down 20 bps QoQ due to rate normalization—tempered growth, but our 4% GPW increase in specialty lines like cyber and D&O kept regional earnings steady. Asia-Pacific shines brightest, with 12% organic growth in life and health reinsurance, fueled by demand for critical illness products amid aging demographics in Japan and Southeast Asia; this segment's 18% ROE directly juices our group-wide dividend pool.

Strategically, we're enhancing shareholder returns through a balanced capital allocation playbook. Complementing the dividend, I'd like to provide an update on our share repurchase activity, which remains a cornerstone of our disciplined framework. In Q3 alone, we executed $450 million in share repurchases, bringing our year-to-date total to $1.2 billion. This represents a 35% acceleration from the $890 million we deployed in the first half of 2023, reflecting our view that shares have been trading at a compelling discount to our embedded value—currently estimated at around 1.4x our adjusted tangible book value per share of $72.50.

We repurchased approximately 5.3 million shares in the quarter at an average price of $85.12, with volumes concentrated in late quarter amid broader market pullbacks. Year-to-date, this equates to 14.1 million shares bought back, reducing our fully diluted shares outstanding by 2.5% to 542 million. This activity was immediately accretive to EPS by approximately 4.2%, and boosted our ROE by 120 basis points on a TTM basis to 14.8%, outperforming the S&P P&C Insurance Index peer average.

We've enhanced execution through a new Rule 10b5-1 trading plan and proprietary algorithmic strategies, minimizing market impact. Regionally, U.S. operations drove 72% of the activity, funded by strong operating cash flow. In Europe, it was more measured due to Solvency II considerations, and Asia-Pacific opportunistic leveraging investment income.

We've also expanded our DRIP, with 22% uptake this quarter. On the technical front, catastrophe modeling partnerships with RMS and Karen Clark & Company have de-risked our portfolio. This supports our goal of 45-50 cents annual dividend growth through the cycle, assuming mid-single-digit EPS expansion.

In summary, our expense trends, cat management, actuarial updates, dividends, and repurchases reflect a virtuous cycle of growth outpacing inflation, positioning us for a sub-95% combined ratio. Thank you—I'll hand it back shortly.

Elena Vasquez: Thank you, Michael. I'd like to provide an update on our underwriting performance. We've seen continued strong performance in our commercial P&C lines. We are actively managing our exposure to catastrophe perils and secondary risks like cyber, and have implemented several initiatives to improve our risk selection, including advanced telematics and AI underwriting tools.

David Kwon: Just briefly, our investment portfolio continues to perform well, with net investment income up 12% year-over-year, driven by higher yields and disciplined duration management amid the rate environment.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Lisa Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen: Good morning. Can you provide more color on the expense ratio drivers and how sustainable the compression is?

Michael Rivera: Good morning, Lisa. Absolutely—the 110 basis point YoY improvement to 28.7% was broad-based, as I detailed, from direct channel shifts to 32% mix and tech efficiencies like 72% STP in claims. Our 2025 target of 27.5% is achievable via GenAI and acquisition synergies, even with macro headwinds.

Operator: Our next question comes from Mark Reilly with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Mark Reilly: Good morning. Could you discuss the impact of catastrophe losses on your business and outlook?

Elena Vasquez: Good morning, Mark. At 4.2% of GWP, down 190 bps YoY, we managed well through reinsurance cessions and modeling upgrades. FY guidance is 3.8-4.2%, supporting mid-teens ROEs.

Operator: Our next question comes from Priya Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Priya Patel: What is the expected impact of actuarial assumption changes on your reserving strategy going forward?

Michael Rivera: Thanks, Priya. The $285 million favorable this quarter, led by discount rates and mortality normalization, reflects mature data and stochastic modeling. Q4 should be neutral to positive $100 million, with ongoing derisking via reinsurance.

Operator: Our next question comes from Tom Bradley with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Tom Bradley: On capital returns, can you elaborate on dividend growth and buyback plans?

Michael Rivera: Certainly, Tom. The $0.68 Q4 dividend, up 4.6% QoQ, with 42% payout and 12-year growth streak, pairs with $1.2 billion YTD repurchases. $2.5 billion remains authorized, opportunistic below $82.

Operator: Our final question comes from Alex Rivera with Citigroup. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: How are regulatory changes like IFRS 17 affecting your expense and assumption updates?

Elena Vasquez: Good question, Alex. IFRS 17 has prompted DAC adjustments aiding expense ratios in EMEA, and refined RA loadings in Asia. We're compliant and leveraging it for better transparency.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you for your questions and your interest in Apex Insurance Holdings. In closing, we are confident in our ability to continue delivering strong results and creating value for our shareholders. Thank you for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
